papers.title: Internal Consistency and Self-Feedback in Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a unified perspective on internal consistency in LLMs, introducing the Self-Feedback framework to categorize methods for improving reasoning and reducing hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes that internal consistency is a key challenge in LLMs and that Self-Feedback methods are promising for improving consistency, but more research is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Internal consistency can be viewed at three levels: response, decoding, and latent, and follows an hourglass evolution pattern.
Self-Feedback, consisting of Self-Evaluation and Self-Update, is an effective framework for mining internal consistency.
The survey categorizes existing methods into lines of work for reasoning elevation and hallucination alleviation.
The paper proposes the 'Consistency Is (Almost) Correctness' hypothesis and 'The Paradox of Latent and Explicit Reasoning'.
The survey addresses the question 'Does Self-Feedback Really Work?' with an in-depth analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit deficient reasoning or generate hallucinations. To address these, studies prefixed with "Self-" such as Self-Consistency, Self-Improve, and Self-Refine have been initiated. They share a commonality: involving LLMs evaluating and updating themselves. Nonetheless, these efforts lack a unified perspective on summarization, as existing surveys predominantly focus on categorization. In this paper, we use a unified perspective of internal consistency, offering explanations for reasoning deficiencies and hallucinations. Internal consistency refers to the consistency in expressions among LLMs' latent, decoding, or response layers based on sampling methodologies. Then, we introduce an effective theoretical framework capable of mining internal consistency, named Self-Feedback. This framework consists of two modules: Self-Evaluation and Self-Update. The former captures internal consistency signals, while the latter leverages the signals to enhance either the model's response or the model itself. This framework has been employed in numerous studies. We systematically classify these studies by tasks and lines of work; summarize relevant evaluation methods and benchmarks; and delve into the concern, "Does Self-Feedback Really Work?" We also propose several critical viewpoints, including the "Hourglass Evolution of Internal Consistency", "Consistency Is (Almost) Correctness" hypothesis, and "The Paradox of Latent and Explicit Reasoning". The relevant resources are open-sourced at https://github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/ICSFSurvey.

papers.title: Temporal Predictors of Outcome in Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: The chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm uses the elicitation of step-by-step rationales as a proxy for reasoning, gradually refining the model's latent representation of a solution. However, it remains unclear just how early a Large Language Model (LLM) internally commits to an eventual outcome. We probe this by training linear classifiers on hidden states after the first t reasoning tokens, showing that eventual correctness is highly predictable after only a few tokens, even when longer outputs are needed to reach a definite answer. We show that, for harder questions, a drop in predictive accuracy highlights a selection artifact: hard items are disproportionately represented in long CoTs. Overall, our results imply that for reasoning models, internal self-assessment of success tends to emerge after only a few tokens, with implications for interpretability and for inference-time control.

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM confidence estimation by analyzing the stability of internal representations under targeted adversarial perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CCPS, a method that estimates LLM confidence by analyzing the stability of internal representations under adversarial perturbations, achieving significant improvements in calibration and discrimination metrics across diverse models and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CCPS provides an efficient, accurate, and generalizable method for LLM confidence estimation, enhancing the trustworthiness of LLMs in critical domains.
papers.key_findings:
CCPS reduces average Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% (up to 88%) and Brier score by 21% (up to 45%) compared to the best baseline.
CCPS increases average Accuracy by 5 percentage points, AUCPR by 4 percentage points, and AUROC by 6 percentage points.
CCPS generalizes across diverse LLM architectures (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and model scales (8B to 32B parameters).
CCPS performs well on both multiple-choice and open-ended question answering formats.
CCPS is parameter-efficient, adding only around 9.5k trainable parameters, compared to baselines that may add millions.
papers.abstract: Reza Khanmohammadi, Erfan Miahi, Mehrsa Mardikoraem, Simerjot Kaur, Ivan Brugere, Charese Smiley, Kundan S Thind, Mohammad M. Ghassemi. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Calibration Across Layers: Understanding Calibration Evolution in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does calibration evolve throughout the depth of transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that calibration is a distributed phenomenon across network layers, with a distinct confidence correction phase in later layers, and identifies a low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream that can improve calibration metrics without harming accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Our findings suggest that calibration is a distributed phenomenon, shaped throughout the network’s forward pass, not just in its final projection, providing new insights into how confidence-regulating mechanisms operate within LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Calibration evolves across layers, with a distinct confidence correction phase in later layers where models become overconfident and then recalibrate.
A low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream is identified, and perturbing it improves calibration metrics (ECE and MCE) without affecting accuracy.
The unembedding matrix's null space plays a role in calibration.
Calibration is a distributed phenomenon across the network depth, not just in the final projection.
papers.limitation:
The calibration direction identified in Phi-2 does not generalize effectively to Mistral or LLaMA-2.
The analysis is limited to zero-shot MCQA prompts and may not extend to in-context learning settings.
future_direction: Generalizing calibration directions using gradient-based approaches and verifying alignment with low-rank structures in the unembedding matrix.
Investigating model internals to identify neurons or components that contribute to confidence modulation.
Extending analysis to in-context learning settings and cross-model/dataset transferability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated inherent calibration capabilities, where predicted probabilities align well with correctness, despite prior findings that deep neural networks are often overconfident. Recent studies have linked this behavior to specific components in the final layer, such as entropy neurons and the unembedding matrix null space. In this work, we provide a complementary perspective by investigating how calibration evolves throughout the network depth. Analyzing multiple open-weight models on the MMLU benchmark, we uncover a distinct confidence correction phase in the upper/later layers, where model confidence is actively recalibrated after decision certainty has been reached. Furthermore, we identify a low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream whose perturbation significantly improves calibration metrics (ECE and MCE) without harming accuracy. Our findings suggest that calibration is a distributed phenomenon, shaped throughout the network forward pass, not just in its final projection, providing new insights into how confidence-regulating mechanisms operate within LLMs.

papers.title: Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
papers.research_question: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Specifically, is the structure given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process, and are belief states linearly represented in the residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the geometry of belief states (from the mixed-state presentation of the data-generating process) in their residual stream, even for complex fractal geometries, and that this representation captures information beyond local next-token predictions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers construct predictive representations that encode the complex geometry of belief updating over hidden states, capturing an inference process over the underlying structure of the data-generating process, which provides a concrete link between training data structure and internal model representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov models (HMMs) linearly represent the belief state geometry of the mixed-state presentation in their residual stream, as verified by linear regression.
The belief state representation emerges during training and is not an artifact, as shown by controls including cross-validation and shuffling.
For processes where distinct belief states share the same next-token distribution (e.g., RRXOR), the belief state geometry is not well represented in the final layer alone but is distributed across multiple layers of the residual stream.
The representation captures information about the entire future distribution, not just the next token, as demonstrated by comparing pairwise distances between belief states versus next-token probabilities.
The belief state geometry is robust to the choice of using pre- or post-layer normalization activations.
papers.limitation:
Experimental validation focused on small-scale systems (HMMs with 3-5 states and vocabularies of 2-3 tokens), a significant simplification compared to modern language models.
For realistic systems, the dimensionality of the belief state simplex would exceed the residual stream dimension, suggesting representation must be compressed; the nature of this compression is not understood.
Explicitly computing ground-truth belief states becomes intractable as the size of the minimal generating structure and context window length grows, requiring new methodologies for validation in larger settings.
The work is limited to the stationary ergodic setting, though the framework is expected to extend to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes.
The paper establishes the representation of belief states but does not test whether transformers implement a circuit for performing Bayesian updates.
future_direction: Extending the framework to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes, such as in-context learning.
Understanding how belief state geometry is compressed when the simplex dimension exceeds the residual stream dimension.
Investigating the mapping between belief states and features, which is likely complex and architecture-dependent.
papers.abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

papers.title: LENS: Learning Ensemble Confidence from Neural States for Multi-LLM Answer Integration
papers.research_question: How can we effectively combine predictions from multiple LLMs by learning to estimate each model's context-dependent confidence from its internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LENS, a novel ensemble method that learns lightweight linear confidence predictors for each LLM using layer-wise hidden states and normalized probabilities, enabling more effective weighting of model predictions based on context-dependent reliability.
papers.conclusion: LENS is a simple yet effective ensemble method that leverages model confidence patterns learned from internal representations to improve performance across diverse question-answering tasks, offering a practical and scalable solution for robust LLM ensembles.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Max Confidence ensemble method outperforms baseline methods (Majority Vote and Probability Max) on 5 out of 6 evaluated datasets.
Internal representations (hidden states) contain valuable signals for determining model confidence and can be effectively leveraged for ensemble learning.
The method is simple to implement, computationally efficient, and does not require retraining or modifying the base LLMs.
The approach generalizes well across diverse question-answering tasks, including logical reasoning, commonsense inference, and mathematics.
papers.limitation:
The current implementation is restricted to decoder-only transformer architectures, limiting applicability to encoder-decoder or other model types.
The method requires access to intermediate layer representations, which may not be available in production environments or with commercial API-based models.
future_direction: Investigating cross-task transferability of learned confidence patterns for zero-shot ensemble learning.
Extending the method to modern multi-LLM systems and agent collaboration scenarios.
Leveraging confidence patterns and intermediate representations to enhance understanding of LLM decision-making processes (model interpretability).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across various tasks, with different models excelling in distinct domains and specific abilities. Effectively combining the predictions of multiple LLMs is crucial for enhancing system robustness and performance. However, existing ensemble methods often rely on simple techniques like voting or logits ensembling, which overlook the varying confidence and reliability of models in different contexts. In this work, we propose LENS (Learning ENsemble confidence from Neural States), a novel approach that learns to estimate model confidence by analyzing internal representations. For each LLM, we train a lightweight linear confidence predictor that leverages layer-wise hidden states and normalized probabilities as inputs. This allows for more nuanced weighting of model predictions based on their context-dependent reliability. Our method does not require modifying the model parameters and requires negligible additional computation. Experimental results on multiple-choice and boolean question-answering tasks demonstrate that LENS outperforms traditional ensemble methods by a substantial margin. Our findings suggest that internal representations provide valuable signals for determining model confidence and can be effectively leveraged for ensemble learning.

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Thinking About Thinking: SAGE-nano's Inverse Reasoning for Self-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to introspect on and explain their own reasoning processes, specifically why they choose particular reasoning chains over alternatives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces inverse reasoning, a paradigm enabling LLMs to introspect on their own reasoning processes via attention pathway reconstruction, and presents SAGE-nano, a 4B-parameter model that demonstrates this capability, improving both reasoning transparency and performance.
papers.conclusion: The inverse reasoning paradigm enables LLMs to introspect on their reasoning and generate interpretable explanations, enhancing transparency and trustworthiness while maintaining competitive performance, establishing foundations for transparent AI systems in safety, education, and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE-nano achieves competitive reasoning accuracy (e.g., 74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and high explanation quality (92.1% human preference score).
Inverse reasoning enhances both reasoning transparency and forward reasoning performance, as shown by ablation studies.
The model demonstrates superior introspection accuracy in identifying decision points, alternative paths, and confidence calibration.
The architecture can be trained and deployed efficiently on consumer hardware (Mac Mini M1 cluster), making advanced reasoning more accessible.
Inverse reasoning addresses critical AI safety challenges by providing interpretable explanations of model decision-making.
papers.limitation:
The inverse reasoning approach adds significant computational overhead (40% inference time), limiting scalability to larger models.
Current metrics for explanation quality rely heavily on subjective human evaluation; developing automated evaluation metrics remains an open problem.
Inverse reasoning explanations lack objective ground truth, making validation difficult.
The 4-billion parameter constraint limits the model's capacity for complex reasoning tasks compared to larger state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Investigating inverse reasoning capabilities in larger model architectures (scalability studies).
Extending inverse reasoning to visual and multi-modal reasoning tasks.
Developing robust automated metrics for explanation quality assessment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities at solving complex reasoning tasks with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, but their decision-making processes remain somewhat blackbox. We introduce textbfinverse reasoning, a novel paradigm enabling LLMs to decompose and explain their own reasoning chains post-hoc. Our approach, used in SAGE-nano, a 4-billion-parameter reasoning model, employs a metacognitive structure that reflects back via attention processes to identify major decision points and generate explanations of reasoning choices. While typical CoT approaches are directed towards forward reasoning generation, inverse reasoning provides insight into why specific reasoning chains were selected over others. Through thorough testing of logical reasoning puzzles, math problems and ethical dilemmas from AQUA-RAT, CommonsenseQA, and customized benchmarks, we demonstrate that SAGE-nano is at the cutting edge both on reasoning accuracy (74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and explanation quality (92.1% human preference score) for its task, and offers performance almost on par with models like Claude-3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4o. Our contributions are: (i) the first rigorous framework for LLM self-reflection via inverse reasoning, (ii) a novel metalearning framework to reverse the attention flow, (iii) comprehensive evaluation frameworks for reasoning transparency, and (iv) evidence that increasing reasoning using inverse reasoning improves interpretability along with reasoning performance. Our work creates new avenues for transparent AI systems and closes significant gaps in AI safety, education, and scientific discovery.

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent and track characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a pervasive 'lookback mechanism' that language models use to track characters' beliefs, and introduces the CausalToM dataset for causal analysis of Theory of Mind.
papers.conclusion: The lookback mechanism is a foundational computation for belief tracking in language models, providing a step toward reverse-engineering Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Language models use a systematic 'lookback mechanism' for belief tracking, which involves recalling important information when needed.
The mechanism uses Ordering IDs (OIs) to bind character-object-state triples in the residual stream of state tokens.
Three key lookbacks are identified: binding lookback (retrieves state OI), answer lookback (retrieves state token), and visibility lookback (updates beliefs based on visibility).
The mechanism generalizes across model scales (70B to 405B) and model families (Llama and Qwen).
The visibility lookback uses a visibility ID to retrieve information about observed characters and update the observing character's beliefs.
papers.limitation:
The visibility lookback mechanism is only partially understood and requires further investigation.
The mechanism does not scale to three characters in the visibility condition.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex scenarios with more characters and objects.
Further investigation of the visibility lookback mechanism.
Applying the lookback mechanism analysis to other tasks and domains.
papers.abstract: How do language models (LMs) represent characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality? This question lies at the heart of understanding the Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities of LMs. We analyze LMs' ability to reason about characters' beliefs using causal mediation and abstraction. We construct a dataset, CausalToM, consisting of simple stories where two characters independently change the state of two objects, potentially unaware of each other's actions. Our investigation uncovers a pervasive algorithmic pattern that we call a lookback mechanism, which enables the LM to recall important information when it becomes necessary. The LM binds each character-object-state triple together by co-locating their reference information, represented as Ordering IDs (OIs), in low-rank subspaces of the state token's residual stream. When asked about a character's beliefs regarding the state of an object, the binding lookback retrieves the correct state OI and then the answer lookback retrieves the corresponding state token. When we introduce text specifying that one character is (not) visible to the other, we find that the LM first generates a visibility ID encoding the relation between the observing and the observed character OIs. In a visibility lookback, this ID is used to retrieve information about the observed character and update the observing character's beliefs. Our work provides insights into belief tracking mechanisms, taking a step toward reverse-engineering ToM reasoning in LMs.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive large language models internally represent and process emotional information to infer emotions from text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that emotion representations in LLMs are functionally localized to mid-layers and that causal interventions on appraisal concepts can steer emotion inference in psychologically plausible ways.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a mechanistic understanding of emotion inference in LLMs and demonstrates causal intervention methods to control emotion inference, with potential applications in safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion representations are functionally localized to specific mid-layers across diverse model families and sizes.
Activation patching reveals that MHSA and FFN units in mid-layers are critical for emotion inference.
Attention patterns in mid-layers shift to emotionally loaded tokens.
Appraisal concepts are linearly represented in the model and their modulation can steer emotion inference.
The structure of emotion representations aligns with cognitive appraisal theory from psychology.
papers.limitation: Focusing only on correctly classified examples may introduce bias toward unambiguous emotional content.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promising capabilities in predicting human emotions from text. However, the mechanisms through which these models process emotional stimuli remain largely unexplored. Our study addresses this gap by investigating how autoregressive LLMs infer emotions, showing that emotion representations are functionally localized to specific regions in the model. Our evaluation includes diverse model families and sizes and is supported by robustness checks. We then show that the identified representations are psychologically plausible by drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, a well-established psychological framework positing that emotions emerge from evaluations (appraisals) of environmental stimuli. By causally intervening on construed appraisal concepts, we steer the generation and show that the outputs align with theoretical and intuitive expectations. This work highlights a novel way to causally intervene and precisely shape emotional text generation, potentially benefiting safety and alignment in sensitive affective domains.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Direct Confidence Alignment: Aligning Verbalized Confidence with Internal Confidence In Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we align a Large Language Model's verbalized confidence (expressed in words) with its internal confidence (derived from token probabilities) to improve model transparency and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Direct Confidence Alignment (DCA), a method using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align an LLM's verbalized confidence with its internal confidence, improving transparency. Results show DCA is effective on some model architectures (e.g., Gemma-2-9B-Instruct) but ineffective on others, highlighting the need for model-aware approaches.
papers.conclusion: DCA can improve alignment between verbalized and internal confidence in some LLMs, but its effectiveness varies across architectures, underscoring the need for further improvements and model-aware alignment strategies.
papers.key_findings:
DCA improved confidence alignment metrics (e.g., Spearman's ρ, mean absolute calibration error) consistently for Gemma-2-9B-Instruct across all datasets.
DCA produced mixed results for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct, sometimes degrading alignment and accuracy, indicating the method's effectiveness is model-dependent.
DCA reduced the variance in calibration error (σ_ϵ and σ_M) for most models, suggesting it makes confidence expression more consistent.
DCA had mixed impacts on model accuracy: it increased accuracy for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, decreased it for Mistral-7B-Instruct, and left Gemma-2-9B-Instruct's accuracy largely unchanged.
The effectiveness of DCA appears to be more dependent on model architecture than on the specific task or dataset.
papers.limitation:
The method requires access to internal logits to extract internal confidence, making it inapplicable to closed-source models.
The method relies on the assumption that the model's internal confidence (from token probabilities) is better calibrated than its verbalized confidence, which may not always hold.
DCA can degrade model accuracy because the preference dataset includes incorrect answers, and the method does not directly optimize for correctness.
future_direction: Expanding the method to be compatible with a wider range of model architectures.
Exploring more strategies to improve the alignment between verbalized and internal confidence.
Developing strategies to mitigate the potential degradation of model accuracy caused by DCA.
papers.abstract: Producing trustworthy and reliable Large Language Models (LLMs) has become increasingly important as their usage becomes more widespread. Calibration seeks to achieve this by improving the alignment between the model's confidence and the actual likelihood of its responses being correct or desirable. However, it has been observed that the internal confidence of a model, derived from token probabilities, is not well aligned with its verbalized confidence, leading to misleading results with different calibration methods. In this paper, we propose Direct Confidence Alignment (DCA), a method using Direct Preference Optimization to align an LLM's verbalized confidence with its internal confidence rather than ground-truth accuracy, enhancing model transparency and reliability by ensuring closer alignment between the two confidence measures. We evaluate DCA across multiple open-weight LLMs on a wide range of datasets. To further assess this alignment, we also introduce three new calibration error-based metrics. Our results show that DCA improves alignment metrics on certain model architectures, reducing inconsistencies in a model's confidence expression. However, we also show that it can be ineffective on others, highlighting the need for more model-aware approaches in the pursuit of more interpretable and trustworthy LLMs.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: Theoretical Limitations of Self-Attention in Neural Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What are the theoretical computational capabilities of self-attention to model formal languages, specifically hierarchical structures and periodic finite-state languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that self-attention cannot model periodic finite-state languages (like PARITY) or hierarchical structure (like DYCK) unless the number of layers or heads increases with input length.
papers.conclusion: Self-attention has limited computational power and cannot model periodic regular languages or basic recursion, which theoretically confirms that it is more restricted than recurrent architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers with hard attention cannot recognize the regular language PARITY or the context-free language DYCK.
For soft attention, transformers cannot achieve perfect cross-entropy when modeling distributions over these formal languages.
The limitations hold unless the number of layers or heads grows with the input length.
The results are asymptotic and may not apply to short input sequences.
Self-attention cannot emulate stacks or general finite-state automata, unlike recurrent networks.
papers.limitation: The results are asymptotic, showing mistakes on sufficiently long inputs, but a transformer may perform well on short inputs by using large numbers of layers and heads.
future_direction: Complementing the asymptotic methods with empirical studies or non-asymptotic extensions.
Investigating connections between sensitivity of functions and generalization in feedforward networks.
papers.abstract: Transformers are emerging as the new workhorse of NLP, showing great success across tasks. Unlike LSTMs, transformers process input sequences entirely through self-attention. Previous work has suggested that the computational capabilities of self-attention to process hierarchical structures are limited. In this work, we mathematically investigate the computational power of self-attention to model formal languages. Across both soft and hard attention, we show strong theoretical limitations of the computational abilities of self-attention, finding that it cannot model periodic finite-state languages, nor hierarchical structure, unless the number of layers or heads increases with input length. These limitations seem surprising given the practical success of self-attention and the prominent role assigned to hierarchical structure in linguistics, suggesting that natural language can be approximated well with models that are too weak for the formal languages typically assumed in theoretical linguistics.

papers.title: Enhancing Language Model Factuality via Activation-Based Confidence Calibration and Guided Decoding
papers.research_question: How can calibration techniques be effectively used to enhance the factuality of language models? This paper investigates activation-based confidence calibration and confidence-guided decoding.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ACTCAB, an activation-based calibration method that reduces expected calibration error by up to 39%, and CODEC, a confidence-guided decoding strategy that improves factuality on challenging QA datasets like TruthfulQA.
papers.conclusion: ACTCAB improves calibration by leveraging internal activations, and CODEC uses these confidence scores to guide decoding, significantly improving factuality on challenging datasets like TruthfulQA.
papers.key_findings:
ACTCAB achieves superior calibration performance, reducing average ECE by 39% compared to the best baseline.
CODEC significantly improves factuality on TruthfulQA, increasing True.*Info. by 50% for Llama2-7b.
CODEC is robust across different training data sources and LMs, unlike intervention methods like ITI and RepE.
CODEC introduces a modest decoding speed reduction (less than 14% throughput decrease) while greatly improving factuality.
The ECE loss, which uses soft labels constructed via K-fold cross-validation, significantly improves calibration over binary loss.
papers.limitation:
ACTCAB and CODEC require access to the LM's activations, which may not be feasible for black-box models.
The methods are not explored on generation tasks involving longer forms, such as paragraphs.
Interpretability of the confidence signals and decisions made by CODEC remains challenging.
future_direction: Investigate longer responses in generation tasks to enhance LM trustworthiness in practical use.
Enhance interpretability of the confidence signals and decisions made by CODEC.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: Tuning-Free Accountable Intervention for LLM Deployment -- A Metacognitive Approach
papers.research_question: How can LLMs be equipped with self-aware error identification and correction capabilities without additional parameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CLEAR, a metacognitive framework that enables LLMs to autonomously identify and self-correct errors at inference time without additional tuning, by learning concept-specific sparse subnetworks.
papers.conclusion: CLEAR pioneers a metacognitive approach to LLM deployment, enabling self-correction and interpretability, which enhances trustworthiness and accountability.
papers.key_findings:
CLEAR consistently outperforms baseline methods in concept and task prediction accuracy on multiple datasets.
The framework provides autonomous error detection via logit entropy scrutiny and self-correction via dynamic expert allocation.
CLEAR operates without human intervention or extra parameter tuning, avoiding issues like catastrophic forgetting.
The intervention is interpretable, allowing backtracking from predictions through concepts and subnetworks to the input text.
Ablation studies show the importance of pseudo intervention during training and logit entropy scrutiny for effective metacognition.
papers.limitation:
The choice of backbones is limited by the availability of open-source pretrained Mixture-of-Experts models.
The framework necessitates careful consideration of ethical implications such as data privacy, bias mitigation, and prevention of misuse.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have catalyzed transformative advances across a spectrum of natural language processing tasks through few-shot or zero-shot prompting, bypassing the need for parameter tuning. While convenient, this modus operandi aggravates ``hallucination'' concerns, particularly given the enigmatic ``black-box'' nature behind their gigantic model sizes. Such concerns are exacerbated in high-stakes applications (e.g., healthcare), where unaccountable decision errors can lead to devastating consequences. In contrast, human decision-making relies on nuanced cognitive processes, such as the ability to sense and adaptively correct misjudgments through conceptual understanding. Drawing inspiration from human cognition, we propose an innovative \textit{metacognitive} approach, dubbed \textbf{CLEAR}, to equip LLMs with capabilities for self-aware error identification and correction. Our framework facilitates the construction of concept-specific sparse subnetworks that illuminate transparent decision pathways. This provides a novel interface for model \textit{intervention} after deployment. Our intervention offers compelling advantages: (\textit{i})~at deployment or inference time, our metacognitive LLMs can self-consciously identify potential mispredictions with minimum human involvement, (\textit{ii})~the model has the capability to self-correct its errors efficiently, obviating the need for additional tuning, and (\textit{iii})~the rectification procedure is not only self-explanatory but also user-friendly, enhancing the interpretability and accessibility of the model. By integrating these metacognitive features, our approach pioneers a new path toward engendering greater trustworthiness and accountability in the deployment of LLMs.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: How Does Unfaithful Reasoning Emerge from Autoregressive Training? A Study of Synthetic Experiments
papers.research_question: What constitutes faithful chain-of-thought reasoning and how does unfaithfulness emerge from autoregressive training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic task (AER) to study chain-of-thought faithfulness, finds a critical noise threshold for faithful reasoning due to simplicity bias, and identifies training phases with emergent self-verification.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that unfaithful reasoning emerges when noise exceeds a critical threshold, driven by simplicity bias, and that models develop implicit self-verification through training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Faithful reasoning is possible only when training noise is below a critical threshold.
Simplicity bias explains the threshold: models prefer simpler stepwise reasoning over skip-step reasoning.
Training dynamics exhibit three reasoning modes: stepwise, mixed, skip-step, with a transient increase in prediction entropy in the mixed mode.
Models learn to encode internal uncertainty, suggesting emergent implicit self-verification.
Shortcut features amplify unfaithfulness.
papers.limitation:
Focus on autoregressive training, not reinforcement learning with verifier rewards.
Potential over-generalization of findings beyond the synthetic task.
future_direction: Investigate reinforcement learning with verifier rewards (RLVR).
Apply metrics to LLMs beyond synthetic setting.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning generated by large language models (LLMs) is often unfaithful: intermediate steps can be logically inconsistent or fail to reflect the causal relationship leading to the final answer. Despite extensive empirical observations, a fundamental understanding of CoT is lacking--what constitutes faithful CoT reasoning, and how unfaithfulness emerges from autoregressive training. We study these questions using well-controlled synthetic experiments, training small transformers on noisy data to solve modular arithmetic expressions step by step, a task we term Arithmetic Expression Reasoning. We find that models can learn faithful reasoning that causally follows the underlying arithmetic rules, but only when the training noise is below a critical threshold, a phenomenon attributable to simplicity bias. At higher noise levels, training dynamics exhibit a transition from faithful stepwise reasoning to unfaithful skip-step reasoning via an intermediate mixed mode characterized by a transient increase in prediction entropy. Mechanistic analysis reveals that models learn to encode internal uncertainty by resolving inconsistent reasoning steps, which suggests the emergence of implicit self-verification from autoregressive training.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-Correction in LLMs: Towards Explainable Prompting via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does intrinsic self-correction prompting act as representation steering along interpretable latent directions?
papers.core_contribution: Intrinsic self-correction in LLMs functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by alignment between prompt-induced shifts and steering vectors and causal verification via activation addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings link self-correction prompting to representation steering along interpretable latent directions, highlighting the role of interpretability methods in understanding prompt-driven LLM phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Prompt-induced shifts in self-correction align with steering vectors constructed from contrastive pairs.
Activation injection with steering vectors causally reproduces behavioral changes in toxicity.
Detoxification is effective even with weak prompts, while toxification requires strong prompts.
Most of the behavioral change occurs in the first self-correction round.
Alignment between shifts and vectors peaks in mid-to-late layers for some models.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to toxicity-related behaviors and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other prompt-driven phenomena such as chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Intrinsic self-correction refers to the phenomenon where a language model refines its own outputs purely through prompting, without external feedback or parameter updates. While this approach improves performance across diverse tasks, its mechanism remains unclear. We show that intrinsic self-correction functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by both alignment analysis and activation interventions. To achieve this, we analyze intrinsic self-correction via the representation shift induced by prompting. In parallel, we construct interpretable latent directions with contrastive pairs and verify the causal effect of these directions via activation addition. Evaluating six open-source LLMs, our results demonstrate that prompt-induced representation shifts in text detoxification and text toxification consistently align with latent directions constructed from contrastive pairs. In detoxification, the shifts align with the non-toxic direction; in toxification, they align with the toxic direction. These findings suggest that representation steering is the mechanistic driver of intrinsic self-correction. Our analysis highlights that understanding model internals offers a direct route to analyzing the mechanisms of prompt-driven LLM behaviors.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior
papers.research_question: Can the internal representations of language models predict their eventual behavior before any output token is generated?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on the internal representations of input tokens can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors of language models, and when combined with conformal prediction, provide provable bounds on estimation error for precise early warning systems.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of language models contain information about eventual behavior, and conformal probes can provide reliable early warning systems for various behaviors, enabling efficient and safe deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on hidden states of input tokens can predict instruction-following failures with high consistency, outperforming a fine-tuned BERT baseline.
Conformal probes can detect safety alignment failures (jailbreaking) and reduce jailbreak success rate from 30% to 2.7%, a 91% reduction.
Probes can preemptively estimate an LM's confidence as measured by per-token perplexity, a behavior that cannot be inferred from output text alone.
When applied to CoT prompting for text classification, conformal probes reduce inference costs by 65% on average across 27 datasets with negligible accuracy loss.
Probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting favorable scaling properties.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on the exchangeability assumption for conformal prediction, which may not hold in practice.
The method was only tested on a few datasets and with a few runs.
papers.abstract: The text produced by language models (LMs) can exhibit specific `behaviors,' such as a failure to follow alignment training, that we hope to detect and react to during deployment. Identifying these behaviors can often only be done post facto, i.e., after the entire text of the output has been generated. We provide evidence that there are times when we can predict how an LM will behave early in computation, before even a single token is generated. We show that probes trained on the internal representation of input tokens alone can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors over the entire output sequence. Using methods from conformal prediction, we provide provable bounds on the estimation error of our probes, creating precise early warning systems for these behaviors. The conformal probes can identify instances that will trigger alignment failures (jailbreaking) and instruction-following failures, without requiring a single token to be generated. An early warning system built on the probes reduces jailbreaking by 91%. Our probes also show promise in pre-emptively estimating how confident the model will be in its response, a behavior that cannot be detected using the output text alone. Conformal probes can preemptively estimate the final prediction of an LM that uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, hence accelerating inference. When applied to an LM that uses CoT to perform text classification, the probes drastically reduce inference costs (65% on average across 27 datasets), with negligible accuracy loss. Encouragingly, probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting applicability to the largest of models in real-world settings.

papers.title: Curved Inference: A Guide to Geometric Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do token representations evolve geometrically in the residual stream of transformer-based language models, and how does this geometry relate to semantic structure and complex behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Curved Inference framework, a geometric approach to interpretability that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream, demonstrating that these trajectories reflect semantic structure and are associated with behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling.
papers.conclusion: Curved Inference provides a geometric framework for interpretability that shifts focus from static attribution to dynamic inference analysis, offering a model-faithful lens to understand internal computation in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream trajectories are semantically sensitive and show structured curvature in response to concern-shifted prompts.
Residual geometry diverges in cases of latent behavioral shifts, such as deception in sleeper agents, and can precede output changes.
Curvature is functionally associated with sustained self-modeling, persisting even under curvature-penalizing fine-tuning.
Geometric metrics like curvature, salience, and semantic surface area provide reproducible signals across multiple domains.
The residual stream is the exclusive locus for this geometric signal, unlike attention or MLP outputs.
papers.limitation:
Geometric derivatives rely on interpolation assumptions that may not hold in all cases.
Dependence on external LLM classifiers for alignment and intent judgments introduces biases.
Experiments were conducted on models up to 3b parameters, so results may not generalize to larger or opaque systems.
future_direction: Scale testing with larger models
Extending analysis to tasks involving reasoning, planning, or complex dialogue
Formalizing curvature signatures for specific generative behaviors
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a unified framework for analyzing the internal geometry of inference in transformer-based language models. Building on a series of prior studies, we present a consolidated introduction to “Curved Inference”: a methodology that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream as geometric trajectories. Using metrics such as curvature, salience, and semantic surface area, we show that residual trajectories reflect meaningful semantic structure, and are empirically associated with emotional and moral concern, covert intent in sleeper agents, and computational self-modeling dynamics. We consolidate these findings into a reproducible, falsifiable pipeline, supported by formal mathematical definitions and open-source tools. This geometric approach shifts the focus of interpretability from static attribution to dynamic, modelnative inference analysis. The results provide evidence that residual stream geometry is not only measurable, but also structurally related to complex behaviors in the models we study. We invite researchers to replicate, extend, or falsify these claims and test the boundaries of curved inference as a new paradigm for model understanding. Received: 6 August 2025 | Revised: 12 January 2026 | Accepted: 21 January 2026 Conflicts of Interest The author declares that he has no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in GitHub at https://github.com/robman/FRESH-model/tree/main/ benchmarks/curved-inference. Author Contribution Statement Rob Manson: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration.

papers.title: Tracing Facts or just Copies? A critical investigation of the Competitions of Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in LLMs mediate the competition between factual recall from parametric memory and counterfactual information provided in context? Do they perform selective counterfactual suppression or general copy suppression, and are they domain-specific?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads that promote factual output in LLMs operate via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, and their behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models showing more specialization.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that attention heads mediate the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens via copy suppression, and their effects are domain-dependent, with implications for model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads contribute to the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens, and modifying their strength affects the proportion of factual outputs.
The attention heads supporting factual tokens suppress copying in general, not just counterfactuals, as they also suppress factual tokens when facts are present in the prompt.
The effect of attention heads is sensitive to sentence structure and the presence of hints (factual token in the subject).
Attention heads exhibit domain specialization; their contribution varies by answer category (e.g., location, language, organization).
Larger models (Pythia-6.9B) show more specialized and category-sensitive patterns than smaller models (GPT-2).
papers.limitation: The experiments are limited to two models (GPT-2 and Pythia-6.9B) and do not cover more models or study attention modification of different heads on different domains in detail.
future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: Knowing When to Stop: Efficient Context Processing via Latent Sufficiency Signals
papers.research_question: Can we enable LLMs to self-assess context sufficiency and terminate early without compromising accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces dynamic context cutoff, a method that uses internal sufficiency signals in attention heads to enable LLMs to stop processing context early, achieving token reduction and accuracy improvement.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic context cutoff enables LLMs to process only minimal necessary context by detecting sufficiency signals internally, reducing tokens by 1.33× and improving accuracy by 3.4%, outperforming static methods.
papers.key_findings:
Specific attention heads encode latent sufficiency signals detectable via lightweight classifiers.
The method achieves an average token reduction of 1.33× and accuracy improvement of 3.4%.
Larger models (14B+) exhibit emergent self-assessment capabilities through prompting.
The method outperforms static context compression methods like RAG and LLMLingua.
Sufficiency detection is more reliable through internal activations than surface-level outputs.
papers.limitation:
Applicability to all task types (e.g., creative writing, open-ended dialogue) remains an open question.
Relies on validation-based hyperparameter tuning for threshold selection.
future_direction: Investigate classifier performance across broader task spectrums.
Develop adaptive threshold selection mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process entire input contexts indiscriminately, which is inefficient when the information required to answer a query is localized within the context. We present dynamic context cutoff, a novel method enabling LLMs to self-terminate processing upon acquiring sufficient task-relevant information. Through analysis of model internals, we discover that specific attention heads inherently encode "sufficiency signals" -- detectable through lightweight classifiers -- that predict when critical information has been processed. This reveals a new efficiency paradigm: models' internal understanding naturally dictates processing needs rather than external compression heuristics. Comprehensive experiments across six QA datasets (up to 40K tokens) with three model families (LLaMA/Qwen/Mistral, 1B-70B) demonstrate 3.4% accuracy improvement while achieving 1.33x token reduction on average. Furthermore, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to other context efficiency methods at equivalent token reduction rates. Additionally, we observe an emergent scaling phenomenon: while smaller models require probing for sufficiency detection, larger models exhibit intrinsic self-assessment capabilities through prompting.

papers.title: Introspection for convolutional automatic speech recognition
papers.research_question: How can common introspection techniques from computer vision be applied to Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), and what difficulties arise? The paper also proposes a new method to overcome these difficulties.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes NAvAI, a data-driven global introspection method that averages and aligns input spectrograms to reveal interpretable, letter-specific patterns learned by a CNN for speech recognition.
papers.conclusion: Applying common image-based introspection techniques to ASR is not straightforward due to challenges with input data interpretability and architectural differences. The proposed NAvAI method offers a viable approach for global introspection in ASR by revealing letter-specific patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Local introspection methods (sensitivity analysis and LRP) applied to the ASR model do not provide clear, interpretable insights into letter-specific patterns.
Activation maximization produces interpretable patterns only for neurons in lower network layers; optimal inputs for higher layers are unnatural and uninterpretable.
The proposed NAvAI method, which averages aligned spectrogram frames predicted as the same letter and normalizes by the mean over all letters, successfully reveals interpretable letter-specific patterns (e.g., formants for vowels, release bursts for plosives).
